source_text:
καὶ οὐ
νόμον τηρεῖ· πέπαυται γάρ. πτωχὰ δὲ στοιχεῖα εἰπὼν οὐ κατηγόρησεν ὡς πονηρῶν,
ἀλλ' ὡς πλουτίζειν μὴ δυναμένων καὶ ἀρκεῖν πρὸς εὐσέβειαν. 302 Gal 4,12 Μὴ
νομίσητε, φησίν, ὅτι ἄλλην τινὰ λύπην εἶχον πρὸς ὑμᾶς καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἐπιπλήττω·
τῆς γὰρ ὀδύνης τὸ πάθος συνεχῶς αὐτὸν μεταβάλλειν ἀναγκάζει τοῦ λόγου τὸ εἶδος,
καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐπιτιμᾶν, νῦν δὲ παρακαλεῖν, καὶ ποτὲ μὲν κατηγορεῖν, ποτὲ δὲ θρηνεῖν.
ἐνταῦθα τοίνυν διδάσκει ὡς ἅπερ γράφει, διὰ φιλοστοργίαν γράφει–οὐδὲν γάρ, φησί,
παρ' ὑμῶν ἠδίκημαι–, ἀλλὰ καὶ θεραπείαν, ὅτι μάλιστα πλείστης ἠξίωμαι. Gal 4,15–
18 Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός; ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς. ἢ οὕτως· τὸ τηρεῖν νόμον ἢ τὸ πίστει ζῆν;
καὶ ἐπειδὴ εἶπεν ὅτι ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἵνα τὸ τέλειον αὐτοὶ ἔχωσι
τῆς πίστεως μὴ τηροῦντες νόμον, ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἐπήγαγεν ὅτι ταῦτα
λέγω οὐ φθονῶν αὐτοῖς· ὤφελον γὰρ κἀκεῖνοι τέλειοι ἦσαν τῇ πίστει κεχρημένοι,
καὶ ἀκώλυτον ἦν αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς. καὶ ὑμεῖς οὖν τοιαῦτα
πράττετε ἃ καὶ ζηλωτοὺς ὑμᾶς ποιεῖ, ἵνα πάντες ὑμᾶς μιμῶνται, καὶ μὴ ὅταν ἔλθω
αἰδεσθέντες με τοιοῦτοι γίνεσθε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμοῦ μὴ παρόντος ἑαυτοὺς διορθοῦσθε.
Gal 4,23–24 Νῦν τῷ ὀνόματι κατεχρήσατο, οὐ τῇ δυνάμει τῆς ἀλληγορίας. ἡ γὰρ
ἀλληγορία οὐ στοιχεῖ τοῖς ῥητοῖς, ἄλλα δέ τινα ἐμφαινόμενα ἀπὸ τῆς κατὰ τὴν ὑφὴν
τῶν νοημάτων ἀκολουθίας εἰσάγει, οἷόν ἐστι τὸ φιλησάτω με ἀπὸ φιλημάτων
στόματος αὐτοῦ, τοῦ ἐν τοῖς Ἄσμασι τῶν Ἀσμάτων· ἐκεῖ γὰρ οὔτε φίλημα οὔτε θρὶξ
οὔτε κοιλία οὐδὲ μηροὶ οὐδὲ ἕτερόν τι, ἀλλ' ἄλλα δι' ἄλλων εἰσάγεται, καὶ τοῦτό
ἐστιν ἀλληγορίας εἶδος κύριον. ἐνταῦθα δὲ καὶ ἡ ἱστορία ὡμολόγηται, καὶ ὅτι τύπος
ἐστὶ τοῦ μέλλοντος ἀποδέδεικται. ἡ οὖν δι' ἔργων προφητεία ἀλληγορία νῦν
ὠνόμασται. τῶν γὰρ προφητειῶν αἱ μέν εἰσι διὰ λόγων μόνον ὡς τὸ ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος
ἐν γαστρὶ λήψεται, αἱ δὲ δι' ἔργων μόνον ὡς Μωϋσῆς ὕψωσε τὸν ὄφιν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ,
αἱ δὲ καὶ δι' ἔργων καὶ διὰ λόγων ὡς τὸ πρὸς 303 Ἰερεμίαν ῥηθέν, τὸ λάβε περίζωμα
καινὸν καὶ περίθου· εἶτα θάψον αὐτὸ παρὰ τὸν Εὐφράτην, καὶ ὡς διερρύη τῷ χρόνῳ
καὶ διεβρώθη, λάβε αὐτό, φησίν, ἐκεῖθεν. ἕως γὰρ τούτου δι' ἔργων ἡ προφητεία, τὸ
δὲ ἑξῆς καὶ διὰ λόγων· ὅτι οὕτως κἀγὼ τοὺς υἱοὺς Ἰσραὴλ περιεθέμην καὶ οὕτως
αὐτοῖς ἐβοήθησα, καὶ οὕτως αὐτοὺς εἰς Βαβυλῶνα ἀπάγω αἰχμαλώτους καὶ
σαθρωθέντας καὶ φθαρέντας ἐκεῖθεν ἀναγάγω καὶ ἀποκαθιστῶ.
thought_title: Rebuke from affection and prophecy through events
orientation: Paul is defending his sharp and shifting tone toward the Galatians and explaining what he means by allegory about Hagar and Sarah.
pass_a_gloss: and he does not keep law; for it has ceased. And having called them poor elemental things, he did not accuse them as evil, but as not being able to make rich and to suffice for reverence. Gal 4,12 Do not suppose, he says, that I had some other grief against you and for this reason I rebuke; for the suffering of his anguish compels him continually to change the form of his speech, both now to rebuke, now to exhort, and at one time to accuse, at another to lament. Here then he teaches that what he writes, he writes through affection — for, he says, in nothing have I been wronged by you —, but also because of care, because I have been judged worthy of the greatest. Gal 4,15-18 What then is the blessedness? instead of none. Or thus: to keep law or to live by faith? And since he said that those men want not to make you zealous, in order that they themselves may have the perfection of faith while not keeping law, but themselves to make you zealous, he added that I say these things not envying them; for would that those men also were perfect having used faith, and it was unhindered for them to be emulated and to imitate us. And you therefore do such things which also make you enviable, in order that all may imitate you, and do not, when I come, having felt shame before me, become such, but even when I am not present, correct yourselves. Gal 4,23-24 Now he misused the name, not the power of allegory. For allegory does not follow the spoken words, but introduces other things appearing from the sequence of the thoughts according to the weaving, such as is let him kiss me from the kisses of his mouth, the one in the Song of Songs; for there neither kiss nor hair nor belly nor thighs nor any other thing, but other things are introduced through other things, and this is the proper form of allegory. But here both the history has been acknowledged, and that it is a type of the future has been proved. The prophecy through deeds therefore has now been named allegory. For of the prophecies some are through words only as behold the virgin shall conceive in the womb, and some through deeds only as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, and some both through deeds and through words as the word spoken to Jeremiah, take a new girdle and put it on; then bury it by the Euphrates, and as in time it rotted through and was eaten through, take it, he says, from there. For until this the prophecy is through deeds, and what follows is also through words: that thus also I clothed the sons of Israel around and thus I helped them, and thus I lead them away to Babylon as captives and, having rotted and having been destroyed, I will lead them up from there and restore them.

choices.why: brief glossary requires elemental things for old-order observances
brief glossary requires law for Mosaic bodily commands
brief glossary requires faith for faith in Christ

pass_b_english: He no longer keeps the law, for it has ceased. When Paul calls them poor elemental things, Severianus says, he does not condemn them as evil. He means they cannot enrich anyone or suffice for reverence. Then Paul says, "Do not suppose that I held some other grievance against you and rebuke you for that reason." The passion of his grief continually forces him to change the form of his speech, now to rebuke, now to exhort, now to accuse, and now to lament.

Here, then, he teaches that whatever he writes, he writes from affection. "For," Paul says, "you have done me no wrong." He writes also because of their care, since, as he says, he has been deemed worthy of the very greatest care. Then, "What is your blessedness?" means there is none left. Or it means this: is it keeping the law, or is it to live by faith? And since Paul said those men do not want to emulate you, so that they might have the perfection of faith by not keeping the law, but want you to emulate them, he added, "I say this not from envy toward them. Would that they too were perfect in the use of faith, for then it would be open to them both to be emulated and to imitate us." So you too should act in ways that make you worth emulating, so that all may imitate you. Do not become such people only out of shame when I come, but correct yourselves even when I am absent.

At this point Paul used the name of allegory loosely, not its true meaning. For allegory does not follow the letter. It brings in one set of things made visible through another, by the connected sense running through the texture, as in, "Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth" in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 1:2). There there is no kiss, no hair, no belly, no thighs, nor anything of that kind. One thing is introduced through another, and this is allegory in the strict sense. Here, by contrast, the history is acknowledged, and it is also shown to be a type of what was to come. So prophecy through events is now called allegory.

For some prophecies come through words alone, as, "Behold, the virgin shall conceive" (Isaiah 7:14). Others come through events alone, as when Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness (John 3:14). Still others come through both events and words, as in what was said to Jeremiah: take a new girdle and put it around you, then hide it by the Euphrates, and after it rotted and decayed with time, take it from there (Jeremiah 13:1-7). Up to that taking, the prophecy runs through events. What follows runs also through words. God says that so He clothed the sons of Israel about Himself, and so He helped them, and so He leads them captive to Babylon, and when they have rotted and decayed, He brings them up from there and restores them.

problems.quote: And since Paul said those men want to make you zealous for themselves, so that they keep the perfection of faith for themselves by not keeping the law while they make you zealous
problems.source_quote: καὶ ἐπειδὴ εἶπεν ὅτι ἐκεῖνοι θέλουσιν οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν, ἵνα τὸ τέλειον αὐτοὶ ἔχωσι τῆς πίστεως μὴ τηροῦντες νόμον, ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν
problems.why: Drops 'not' (οὐχὶ) and reverses who emulates whom; the opponents do not want to emulate the Galatians to gain faith without law, but want the Galatians to emulate them.
problems.fix: And since Paul said those men do not want to emulate you, so that they might have the perfection of faith by not keeping the law, but want you to emulate them

edits.old: those men want to make you zealous for themselves, so that they keep the perfection of faith for themselves by not keeping the law while they make you zealous
edits.new: those men do not want to emulate you, so that they might have the perfection of faith by not keeping the law, but want you to emulate them

fixed: Restored negation and direction per οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν ... ἀλλ' αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν: opponents do not emulate you but want you to emulate them.

problems.why: Greek Τίς means "What," not "Where." Substituting "Where" contradicts the source and breaks Severianus's second interpretation ("is it keeping the law, or is it to live by faith?").
problems.ruling: Source τίς is what/who (ὁ μακαρισμός), not ποῦ; 'Where' misrenders the question and weakens the law-or-faith gloss.

edits.old: Then, "Where is your blessedness?" means there is none left.
edits.new: Then, "What is your blessedness?" means there is none left.

fixed: "Where is your blessedness?" -> "What is your blessedness?": fixed; source has Τίς ογν ο μακαρισμός (What, not Where), fitting the law-or-faith alternative.
'do not want to emulate you ... want you to emulate them': left alone as correct; source οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν ... αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν with αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς reads as emulate/be emulated.

problems.quote: At this point Paul misused the name of allegory, not its power.
problems.source_quote: Νῦν τῷ ὀνόματι κατεχρήσατο, οὐ τῇ δυνάμει τῆς ἀλληγορίας.
problems.why: κατεχρήσατο means 'used loosely' and δυνάμει means 'meaning/force,' not 'power'; 'misused ... not its power' reverses the sense to suggest Paul properly used allegory's power.
problems.fix: At this point Paul used the name of allegory loosely, not its true meaning.
problems.ruling: "Not its power" suggests δύναμις unused rightly; Greek contrasts name (κατεχρήσατο) with allegory's force, not misuse vs. power.

problems.quote: he added that he speaks not from envy toward them. Would that they too were perfect in the use of faith, for then it would be open to them both to be emulated and to imitate us.
problems.source_quote: καὶ ἀκώλυτον ἦν αὐτοὺς ζηλοῦσθαι καὶ μιμεῖσθαι ἡμᾶς.
problems.why: After third-person indirect speech ('he added that he speaks'), the unmarked shift to 'us,' 'you,' and 'I' hides that these are Paul's words rather than Severianus's.
problems.fix: he added, "I say this not from envy toward them. Would that they too were perfect in the use of faith, for then it would be open to them both to be emulated and to imitate us."
problems.ruling: After "he added that he speaks," ὤφελον…ἡμᾶς and ὑμεῖς are Paul's words; unmarked shift can read as Severianus.

problems.quote: He writes also in return for the care of which he says he has been judged most worthy.
problems.source_quote: ἀλλὰ καὶ θεραπείαν, ὅτι μάλιστα πλείστης ἠξίωμαι.
problems.why: πλείστης modifies 'care' ('worthy of the very greatest care'), not 'worthy'; 'judged most worthy' shifts the claim from the Galatians' abundant care to Paul's own worthiness.
problems.fix: He writes also because of their care, since, as he says, he has been deemed worthy of the very greatest care.
problems.ruling: πλείστης genitive: deemed worthy of greatest care (θεραπείαν); "judged most worthy" makes Paul the subject, not the care.

edits.old: At this point Paul misused the name of allegory, not its power.
edits.new: At this point Paul used the name of allegory loosely, not its true meaning.

edits.old: he added that he speaks not from envy toward them. Would that they too were perfect in the use of faith, for then it would be open to them both to be emulated and to imitate us.

fixed: mistranslation allegory: fixed to 'used the name loosely, not its true meaning' per κατεχρήσατο / δυνάμει.
speaker envy: fixed to quoted Paul speech per ταῦτα λέγω οὐ φθονῶν / ὤφελον with I/us.
mistranslation care: fixed to 'worthy of the very greatest care' per πλείστης modifying θεραπείαν.
earlier emulate-you: no edit — οὐχὶ ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν / αὐτοὺς ὑμᾶς ζηλοῦν correctly reads as not emulating you but you emulating them.
earlier What-is-blessedness: no edit — Τίς οὖν ὁ μακαρισμός with ἀντὶ τοῦ οὐδείς correctly reads 'What is your blessedness? means none left'.

last_rejected.quote: those men do not want to emulate you
last_rejected.why: Source: they do not want you emulated; they want you to emulate them.
last_rejected.fix: Those men do not want you to be emulated, so they may keep perfection of faith without keeping the law, but want you to emulate them.
last_rejected.ruling: Active ζηλοῦν (contrast passive ζηλοῦσθαι later) takes ἐκεῖνοι as subject and ὑμᾶς as object, confirmed by ἵνα ... αὐτοὶ ἔχωσι; English is accurate.

last_rejected.quote: to imitate us." So you too should act in ways that make you worth emulating, so that all may imitate you. Do not become such people only out of shame when I come, but correct yourselves even when I am absent.
last_rejected.source_quote: αἰδεσθέντες με τοιοῦτοι γίνεσθε, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐμοῦ μὴ παρόντος ἑαυτοὺς διορθοῦσθε.
last_rejected.why: Closing the quote early leaves Paul's first-person exhortation ("when I come", "when I am absent") outside the quotation marks, as if Severianus were speaking.
last_rejected.fix: to imitate us. So act to be worth emulating, that all may imitate you. Do not become such only out of shame when I come, but correct yourselves even when I am absent."
last_rejected.ruling: ὅταν ἔλθω and ἐμοῦ μὴ παρόντος still clearly Paul; sense preserved; quote end is stylistic in mixed exposition.
